Full text

Abstract

Health misinformation affects individual and public health decisions and erodes trust in medical institutions. Online, people are often confronted with a large variety of both evidencebased and misleading content, making credibility assessments challenging. Judgment errors are not simply the result of a lack of access to accurate information but depend on a variety of cognitive, social and affective factors. In this study, we asked a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population (N = 343) to assess the veracity and credibility of 50 health claims drawn from real-world online information. Using a signal-detection approach, we examined which individual differences predicted accuracy, perceived credibility and response bias.

Results indicate that stronger belief in alternative medicine and in conspiracy theories were associated with lower accuracy, whereas cognitive reflection, motivation for cognition and intellectual humility were not. Stronger belief in alternative medicine, more trust in science, and older age were also associated with being more likely to believe any information regardless of veracity. Overall, our results point towards prior beliefs, not cognitive variables, playing a larger role in what information people choose to believe. Implications for interventions are discussed.

Introduction

When people turn to the internet for information about their health, a large share of what they find may be wrong. This is especially true on social media, where content audits estimate that, depending on platform and topic, between roughly 30% and 87% of health-related social media posts contain misinformation [1]. Exposure to misinformation carries real consequences: misleading claims can negatively influence individual health decisions [2], and more broadly endanger public health, e.g., by undermining vaccination intentions [3], and erode trust in medicine and health institutions [4].

Exposure alone, however, does not automatically equal believing wrong information.

Two people can view the same claim-say a post claiming that vaccines cause autism (a longdebunked claim [5, 6])-and reach completely opposite conclusions regarding its veracity. The psychological processes behind this divergence are still not properly understood, though a large variety of cognitive, social, and affective factors have been proposed [7].

Many interventions have been developed to counter misinformation, but evidence for their effectiveness and real-world usability remains mixed [8, 9]. This could be because errors in judging information can have a large variety of different causes, such as limited health literacy, and a variety of cognitive biases and fallacies (e.g., illusory truth effects [7]), but also a general tendency to overtrust information or excessive skepticism. To design better interventions, we need to identify not just who is more likely to be fooled (i.e., which individual differences are associated with errors, such as lower cognitive reflection or stronger belief in alternative medicine), but also how: Do they struggle to tell true from false claims, or do they have a general disposition to accept (overtrust) or reject (skepticism) claims regardless of veracity? In the present work, we assess the ability of the Austrian population to evaluate a wide range of health (mis)information correctly, using a signal-detection theory (SDT) approach, which addresses both questions.

Signal Detection Approaches in Misinformation

Many misinformation studies use simple scores, such as counting correctly answered items, which conflates whether people can tell true from false claims with their general tendency to accept or reject information [10]. Because laypeople often lack the knowledge to be sure whether a claim is true, judging online information resembles a signal-detection paradigm, since both involve decisions under uncertainty. A SDT framework allows us to separate two otherwise entangled, distinct aspects: People's ability to discriminate true from false information (d'; hereafter accuracy) and their general response bias (c), the general tendency to accept versus reject claims. This distinction has direct practical implications: People with low d′ might benefit from interventions that foster analytic engagement and structured evaluation (e.g., accuracy-nudge interventions [11]), whereas a shifted c might call for threshold recalibration: an overly conservative criterion, for instance, risks rejecting accurate health information whereas an overly liberal one risks accepting misinformation [12].

The Role of Cognition

Dual-process models have a long tradition in psychology (e.g., [13] [14] [15]) and are frequently used to explain why people diverge in their judgments of misinformation [16] [17] [18]. These models propose that judgments can rely either on heuristic, peripheral, or intuitive processing (such as surface markers, source familiarity, or prior attitudes), or on a more effortful and reflective evaluation of the content [19]. According to the Elaboration-Likelihood Model [15], whether a person engages the effortful pathway depends jointly on their ability and their motivation to do so. Applied to misinformation, both are generally assumed to improve accuracy. Consistent with the ability side, performance on the cognitive reflection test (CRT) was positively associated with the ability to discern true from false information in many domains, such as US political news [17], COVID-19 headlines [20], and claims about Russia and Ukraine [21].

To capture the motivation side, it is important to consider motivation for cognition (MFC), people's momentary motivation to engage in effortful thinking [22]. MFC is the state counterpart of the trait need for cognition [23], which has been linked to better detection of fake news [24]. Analytic thinking also reduced unfounded beliefs only among people who were at the same time motivated to hold rational beliefs [25]. Even prompting people to think about accuracy, which may shift their momentary motivation toward accuracy, made them better at distinguishing true from false headlines when deciding what to share [26].

However, this relationship is not always straightforward. Higher need for cognition, for instance, was also associated with stronger belief in the content of conspiracy-theoretical social media posts [27], and a similar pattern emerged for health misinformation among people who relied on social media or alternative health media [28]. This suggests that prior beliefs also shape how accurately people judge information. Particularly relevant for health information are belief in alternative medicine, conspiracy beliefs, and trust in science.

The Role of Prior Beliefs

People tend to accept information that fits their prior beliefs and to doubt information that does not. In political fake news research, partisan biases are well documented: news that is congruent with people's political orientation (e.g., pro-Republican news for conservatives) is accepted more readily than incongruent news [10, 12]. Similar effects occur beyond politics: for topics such as gender-sensitive language and complementary and alternative medicine, laypeople trust study results that conform to their prior beliefs more, while explicit quality signals (e.g., Open Science practices) have no effect [29].

Beliefs about alternative medicine are of particular interest in the context of health information. While some beliefs are relatively harmless, the extreme end of alternative medicine and "natural" healing methods often coincides with a rejection of evidence-based practices, in German derogatorily called "Schulmedizin" (roughly, "conventional mainstream medicine"). Many practices of alternative medicine lack evidence of efficacy [30]. Such beliefs can be assumed to be related to lower accuracy. Consistent with this, positive attitudes towards alternative medicine were among the strongest predictors of susceptibility to health misinformation [31].

Another relevant factor may be conspiracy belief: a general disposition to interpret events as the result of malevolent agents or hidden agency [32]. A typical health-related example is the claim that authorities and pharmaceutical companies conceal the dangers of vaccines [33].

A conspiratorial worldview has also been associated with lower belief in scientific media content [27], so conspiracy belief may be related to lower accuracy.

Finally, people who trust in science should be more likely to follow and believe evidencebased information and thus be more accurate. Consistent with this, higher trust in scientists was associated with lower susceptibility to COVID-19 misinformation [34], and distrust in the health care system predicted greater susceptibility to health misinformation [31].

Motivated Reasoning

Taken together, the importance of beliefs and attitudes points to a limitation of dual-process accounts which largely make lack of reasoning responsible for misjudgments. Yet it is unlikely that people who believe in alternative medicine or conspiracy theories never apply reasoning.

In fact, such beliefs are often accompanied by elaborate (if extremely flawed) argumentation: Alternative healing systems, such as homeopathy, rest on extensive theoretical writings (e.g., Hahnemann's writings on homeopathy), and conspiracy theories can be highly complex [35].

Under motivated reasoning [36], reasoning is directed toward a desired conclusion. Whether this happens when people judge misinformation is debated. Analytic thinking has mostly predicted better discernment, regardless of alignment with participants' own political ideology [17], whereas partisan bias has also been a strong predictor of misinformation susceptibility [37]. This raises the possibility that prior beliefs and cognition do not simply add together in predicting accuracy but can interact: for someone who holds strong beliefs about alternative medicine, cognitive reasoning might not correct wrong beliefs but confirm them further.

Intellectual Humility

A further trait that may affect how people judge health information is intellectual humility: an awareness of the limits of one's own knowledge, and uncertainty about one's own beliefs [38].

In the political domain, it is related to higher openness to the opposing view [38] and predicts more investigative behavior, such as fact checking, in response to information [39]. Its direct relationship to judgments about health information, however, is less clear. It might act as a protective factor, where intellectually humble individuals are more accurate, but they might equally be less certain in their judgments overall.

Response Bias

So far, we have mainly discussed how individual differences might relate to accuracy, as correct discrimination is often the goal when it comes to health information. Some of these individual differences might, however, also affect how readily people accept or reject claims in general, captured by the response bias (c). Most misinformation research has focused solely on accuracy [40] and, to our knowledge, few studies have examined which individual differences relate to response bias. One study found that, for political news, partisan bias was unrelated to discrimination ability and had different correlates, such as subjective confidence instead of cognitive reflection [37]. Another study found that for political and COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, discrimination ability was related to, for example, cognitive reflection and conspiracy mentality, whereas the acceptance threshold showed no robust associations with any of 15 individual difference dimensions [41]. A comparable study found only small associations between individual differences and response bias [20]. For health information beyond COVID-19, however, little is known about this. We therefore examine the relationship between the response bias c and all assessed individual differences in an exploratory way.

The Present Study

Most research on misinformation has focused on political misinformation, often in a US context, with comparatively little work on health information (especially beyond COVID- 19) or non-US samples. In the present study, we investigated individual differences in the ability to discern true and false health information across a large variety of health information contexts in the Austrian population. Based on dual-process accounts, we expected higher cognitive reflection (H1) and higher motivation for cognition (H2) to be associated with higher accuracy and more appropriate credibility ratings, and more positive attitudes towards alternative medicine to be associated with lower accuracy and less appropriate credibility ratings (H3). In line with motivated reasoning, we further expected belief in alternative medicine to attenuate the positive associations of cognitive reflection and motivation for cognition with accuracy and credibility (H4).

For all other predictors, we preregistered open research questions: how intellectual humility, conspiracy belief, and trust in science relate to accuracy and credibility (RQ3-RQ5), which individual differences are associated with response bias (RQ6), and which response patterns to correct and incorrect health information can be distinguished and how individual differences predict them (RQ7). The preregistered hypotheses and full research questions are listed in the Methods.

Methods

Research Questions and Hypotheses

This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) https://osf.io/prt76/overview?view_only=2409483a31c1491eb43996dc6e15c159.

We defined the following research questions (RQs) that are relevant for this paper, along with confirmatory hypotheses (Hs): RQ2: Do positive attitudes toward alternative medicine moderate the positive associations with the other predictor variables? H4: More positive attitudes towards alternative medicine attenuate the positive association of cognitive reflection and motivation for cognition with accuracy and credibility, respectively.

We further formulated exploratory research questions, which are as follows:

RQ3: How does intellectual humility relate to accuracy and credibility ratings? RQ4: How is participants' degree of conspiracy belief related to the accuracy and credibility ratings? RQ5: How is participants' general trust in science related to accuracy and credibility ratings?

RQ6: Which individual differences affect people's response bias c when it comes to evaluating evidence-based health information and health information contrary to the scientific evidence?

Accuracy and bias summarize performance across all items, but people may also differ in how they respond to correct and incorrect information separately, which is not shown by either index alone. Some people might, for example, reliably recognize correct information as true but guess when confronted with incorrect information. We preregistered an approach on how to group people according to response patterns and accordingly formulated RQ7 to describe the population in more detail.

RQ7:

Which response patterns to correct and incorrect health information can be distinguished in the Austrian population, and how do individual differences predict them?

Ethics Information and Informed Consent

The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Graz (GZ. 39/24/63 ex 2025/26) and was carried out in accordance with all relevant guidelines and regulations. All participants gave informed consent before participating.

Participants: Recruitment, Exclusion Criteria, and Sample Size

Participant recruitment took place via the panel provider Talk Online (https://talkonlinepanel.com/) to achieve a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population. Participants were required to be at least 18 years old and speak a sufficient level of German (native speaker or C1 in the European Language Framework). Our target quotas were based on current demographic data derived from Statistik Austria (http://statistik.at/). Quotas were set for participants' age (18-27 years: 13.7%, 28-37 years: 16.7%, 38-47 years: 16.0%, 48-57 years: 17.8%, 58-67 years: 16.4%, 68+ years: 19.4%), gender (approx. 51% female), education (approx. 32% with high school degree or higher), and residential area (approx. 40% rural). We also collected data on participants' political orientation (from "1 -very left", "6 -center", "11 -very right") and net income ("under 1600€", "over 1600€", "over 2300 €", and "over 3000€").

In our preregistration data collection was set to stop at N = 385 (110% of the anticipated sample) prior to exclusion. Following a power calculation in G*Power [42] we aimed for a sample size of N = 350 to detect small effects (corresponding to η² = 0.03, i.e., 3% variance explained; similar to d = 0.34, r = 0.17, β = 0.12, OR = 1.85; [43]) of individual predictors with 90% power at an α error level = 0.05 in a two-sided test in a general linear model. We aimed to analyze between a minimum of 95% (N = 333) and a maximum of 105% (N = 368) of this sample.

A total of 382 participants completed the full survey. According to our preregistration we excluded participants who completed the survey in less than 15 minutes, straight-lined a main questionnaire with reversed items (MFC and HCAMQ), failed the attention check and who self-reported in the end that they got distracted "every so often" or "all the time" during the survey. For our final data analysis, N = 343 remained, which was inside the anticipated range.

Description of Final Sample

Our final sample had an average age of M = 50.51 years (SD = 18.20; min = 18; max = 87), 51.9% were male, 33.6% had a high school (Matura) or university degree, and 42.0% lived in the countryside (less than 10,000 inhabitants in their place of residence). This approximated a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population regarding these demographic markers.

Materials

Questionnaires

The items of questionnaires that are originally in English and had no German translation available (CRT and CAM) were translated into German by one of the study authors, who's native and second language are German and English. Translations were then compared to those of the AI-based language translation tool DeepL. The order of items within all questionnaires was randomized. All scales used in the study were presented on a 1 to 7 rating scale, keeping the original scale labels. The full survey can be found on the osf (osf.io/syd5u/) and our translated questionnaires in the supplementary material.

Motivation for Cognition

Motivation for Cognition was measured with the Motivation for Cognition (MFC) Scale [22]. This scale was originally constructed in German and has 10 items (e.g., "Right now, I would really enjoy a task that involves coming up with new solutions to problems."). Items are scored on a scale of 1 (does not apply at all) to 7 (applies exactly). Scale reliability was good with Cronbach's α = .85.

Ability for Cognitive Reflection

Ability for Cognitive Reflection (CR) was measured using the CRT-MQ-4 [44], of which we used six of the original seven Cognitive Reflection Tasks, where we summed up the correct answers to a 7-point scale consistent with the length of the other rating scales. Items had a fouroption multiple choice answer format which contained the correct answer, an intuitive but wrong alternative and two distractors. (Example item: "Jerry received both the 15th highest and the 15th lowest mark in the class. How many students are in the class? "1 = 29 students (correct answer),2 = 30 students (intuitive answer),3 = 1 student,4 = 15 students).

Belief in Alternative Medicine

Belief in alternative medicine was measured via the Complementary and Alternative Medicine (CAM) subscale of the larger Holistic Complementary and Alternative Medicine Questionnaire (HCAMQ) [45]. These six items measure beliefs about the scientific validity of CAM (e.g., "Complementary medicine should only be used as a last resort when conventional medicine has nothing to offer"). Responses to each item were made on a 7-point rating scale ranging from "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree". Items were re-coded in such a way that a high score indicates stronger belief in CAM and a low score rejection of it. Scale reliability was sufficient with Cronbach's α = .78.

Trust in Science

Trust in Science was measured with five items on public trust in scientists [46] (e.g., "Scientists can be trusted because they are experienced experts in their particular topic."), rated on a 1(strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) scale. This scale is originally in German. Mean scores were calculated, with higher scores indicating greater trust in science. Scale reliability was excellent with Cronbach's α = .92.

Intellectual Humility

Intellectual Humility was measured with the Intellectual Humility Scale [47]. This scale measures Intellectual Humility with 6 self-assessed items (e.g., "I am willing to admit it if I don't know something") on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). The scale reliability was good with Cronbach's α = .85.

Conspiracy Beliefs

Conspiracy beliefs were measured with two items [48, 49] (e.g., "Certain significant events have been the result of the activity of a small group who secretly manipulate world events."), rated on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) scale. Mean scores were calculated, with higher scores indicating stronger conspiracy beliefs. Scale reliability was acceptable with Cronbach's α = .74 (correlation of the two items: r = .59, p < .001).

Further Measures

Participants further reported how often they used different information sources (e.g., science formats, in-depth news reporting, short videos on social media, and AI) and for each health information item whether they had encountered it before. These variables were preregistered as part of the larger study but are not analyzed in the present paper.

Health Information Stimuli Material

In the main part of the study, participants were presented with short written health information texts, which either contained correct or incorrect information. A piece of information was regarded as correct if there was sufficient evidence in favor of this claim, and incorrect if there was sufficient evidence against it. To maintain objectivity, we referred to the independent medical fact-checking project "Medizin Transparent" (medizin-transparent.at) by the University for Continuing Education Krems. This project is certified by the International Fact Checking Network as well as the European Fact Checking Standards Network (EFCSN). At the time of material collection there were 608 fact checks available on their website regarding information from the domain of health and medicine that are relevant to the Austrian public.

For each claim, the fact-checking team indicated whether it is true or false and how confident they are in the underlying evidence: high ("yes"/"no"), moderate ("likely yes"/"likely not"), or low ("possibly yes"/"possibly not"). True claims where studies showed small effect sizes received the qualifier "a bit" (e.g., "probably yes, a little bit"), and claims without meaningful studies were labelled "no scientific evidence". For our study, we only included claims rated with high or moderate confidence in the study results and without the small-effect qualifier, that is, claims rated "yes" or "likely yes" (correct information) and "no" or "likely not" (incorrect information). At the time of material creation, this left 60 pieces of information that we categorized as correct and 59 that we categorized as incorrect. From this pool we excluded information regarding impermanent and current medical events such as information regarding the COVID-19 pandemic as well as false information that could do substantial harm if believed (e.g., recommending a natural product such as ginger instead of chemotherapy to treat cancer).

To create the initial texts, we collected 1 to 2 real webpages or articles that displayed the information for each item. From these, we extracted the main "fact", e.g., "Taking vitamin C regularly prevents the common cold" (incorrect), and between 2 and 3 arguments that explained or supported the fact, e.g., "Vitamin C works as an antioxidant by fighting free radicals". Based on this material, initial texts were created using ChatGPT [50], using a standardized prompt.

The texts were then checked and edited by two of the study's authors. Following this method, we ended up with k = 31 incorrect information texts and k = 35 correct information texts. We tested these in a prestudy of N = 128 people to select the information pieces for the main study (see complete information on the prestudy in the Supplementary Materials). According to the prestudy results we excluded the 6 most extreme false items and the 10 most extreme true items, so we ended up with our final item pool of k = 50 stimuli (k = 25 correct and incorrect, each), which covered a large variety of medical and health-related topics. Participants were presented with the items in a randomized order and answered the following questions after each item: "Do you think this information is true or false?" (1 = "true",0 = "false"), and "How credible do you think this information is?" (1 = "not credible at all" to7 = "very credible").

Additionally, we asked participants if they had heard the information before or not, or if they were unsure or heard the opposite (which is not a relevant variable in this paper).

Procedure Main Study

The study was conducted online using LimeSurvey. Before beginning the study, participants provided informed consent to confirm their voluntary participation and understanding of the study's purpose and procedures. Participants were then asked to provide demographic information concerning their gender, age, nationality, education, place of residence (rural, small town or city), as well as their political orientation and income. The study was quotacontrolled, so that participants belonging to an already filled quota could not complete the study. Following this, participants answered the MFC questionnaire [22] and the CR Test [44].

This was followed by the main part of the study. Participants were presented with a total of 50 items of health-related information. The items appeared one at a time in a randomized order. After each item, participants were asked the three questions pertaining to veracity, credibility and prior exposure. After the tenth item, participants performed an attention check, where they were asked which information they had seen on the previous page and had to select the correct answer out of five answer options. Half of the randomized information items were correct (evidence-based), while the other half were factually incorrect (contrary to the currently available evidence). After rating all 50 items, participants were presented with the other questionnaires in the following order: CAM-scale, trust in science, intellectual humility, conspiracy belief and media use. Items for each scale were randomized We further asked participants if and how distracted they were during the study and what device they used. This was followed by a debriefing about the veracity of the texts, which participants could download for future reference, which linked back to the fact-checking website medizin-transparent.at.

Calculation of Dependent Variables

For each participant, an accuracy and a bias score was calculated from the binary health information responses according to a SDT approach. Each participant's responses towards the items (i.e., health information items) in the experimental part were categorized (Table 1). For the correct items, "true" responses were categorized as Hits and "false" responses as Misses.

For the incorrect items, "false" responses were categorized as Correct Rejections and "true" responses as False alarms.

From these we calculated the hit rate (HR = Hits/Number of correct items) and the false alarm rate (FR = False Alarms/ Number of incorrect items). To avoid extreme rates, we applied a loglinear correction to the False Alarm and Hit Rates by adding 0.5 to each of the cells [51]. From these we calculated the accuracy value d', which is defined as the standardized difference between the means of the signal absent and signal present or in this case "evidence based" and "not evidence based" items. d' was calculated as follows (equation 1): where z(x) is the quantile function for z distribution, such as that a proportion of 0.5 is standardized to a z score of 0.

The greater d' the more accurately a person can distinguish between correct and incorrect health information, whereas d' values close to zero indicate an inability to distinguish between the information and a chance performance.

The value for response bias was defined as the criterion value c and corresponds to the individual threshold of responding "true" or "false" to all the information presented. c is calculated using the following equation ( 2 Perceived credibility constituted our secondary dependent variable. It was operationalized using the credibility ratings (1 = "not credible at all" to7 = "very credible"), which were information-adjusted so that higher scores indicate ratings in line with the scientific evidence: ratings of correct items remained unchanged, whereas ratings of incorrect items were reverse-coded (e.g., a rating of 7 for an incorrect item became 1).

Response profile groups (RQ7)

To describe how participants responded to correct and incorrect information separately, we additionally classified each participant's HR (proportion of correct items judged as "true") and FR (proportion of incorrect items judged as "true") as below chance, at chance, or above chance, based on the raw proportions. This was done using the standard error of a proportion (SEprop), which is described in the equation (3): SEprop = √(.5 × .5 / kitems)

Under random guessing and with k = 25 items per category, the SEprop is .10. Rates within one SE of .50 were therefore treated as chance level: rates ≤ .40 (≤ 10 of 25 items) were coded -1, rates between .41 and .59 (11-14 items) were coded 0, and rates ≥ .60 (≥ 15 items) were coded +1. For correct information, a hit rate coded +1 indicates performance better than chance (accepting correct information) and -1 performance worse than chance (rejecting it). For false information, performance is defined by correct rejections: a false alarm rate coded -1 indicates better-than-chance performance (rejecting incorrect information), and a false alarm rate coded +1 worse-than-chance performance (accepting it). Crossing the three performance levels for correct and for incorrect information resulted in nine groups, ranging from participants who "followed the scientific evidence" (better than chance for both) to those who "responded contrary to it" (worse than chance for both), who "guessed", who are "naive" (accepting everything) and "skeptical" (rejecting everything) in their profiles. These groups correspond to regions in d′-c space (see Figure 2).

Analysis Approach

All analyses were conducted using R [52] and jamovi [53] using the packages GAMLj [54], TOSTER [55], and ggplot2 [56] for figures. All statistical tests were conducted two-sided with a significance level of .05. As preregistered, we calculated general linear models with the individual predictors and the dependent variables accuracy (d') as regression and credibility ratings as multilevel models with trials (i.e., each health information) nested in participants and compared the effect sizes found in the model to the ones used in the power analysis (corresponding to small effect sizes: η² = 0.03, i.e., 3% variance explained; similar to d = 0.34, r = 0.17, β = 0.12, OR = 1.85). Credibility ratings were analyzed with linear mixed models in which trials (Level 1; N = 17,150) were crossed with participants (N = 343) and items (k = 50), with random intercepts for both participants and items. Models were estimated via REML with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; all Level 2 predictors as well as the dependent variable were z-standardized, so that fixed effects can be interpreted as standardized coefficients (β). We performed additional equivalence (TOST) tests on the predictors for accuracy to determine if the correlation between the variables was equivalent to zero, using the equivalence bounds of r = -.17 and r = .17.

RQ1 Individual Differences in Accuracy and Credibility Ratings

Cognitive Reflection (H1)

Contrary to our hypothesis, CR was not significantly associated with participants' accuracy (d'), r = .08, 95% CI[-.03, .18], p = .151; the equivalence test was statistically equivalent to zero within Δr ± .17, 90%CI[-.01, .166].

Motivation for Cognition (H2)

Similarly, MFC also showed no association with accuracy, r = .07, 95% CI[-.03, .18], p = 0.179; the equivalence test was statistically equivalent to zero within Δr ± .17, 90% CI[-0.02, .16].

Belief in Alternative Medicine (CAM) (H3)

As hypothesized, participants' CAM was negatively associated with their overall accuracy, r = -.28, 95% CI[-.38, -.18], p < .001.

When CR, MFC, and CAM were entered simultaneously, the model was significant, R² = .09, F(3, 339) = 11.00, p <.001 (Table 3). Only CAM predicted accuracy in the hypothesized direction, which we treat as robust evidence for H3: People who held stronger beliefs in alternative medicine were worse at distinguishing true and false health information. Neither CR nor MFC was a significant predictor.

We observed similar patterns for the information-adjusted credibility ratings (H1b-H3b); where higher values correspond to more appropriate ratings. We fitted a linear mixed effects model using CR, MFC and CAM as predictors and credibility ratings as the outcome. The model included random intercepts for participants and items to account for the crossed structure of the data (N = 343, k = 50, 17,150 observations in total). The model explained 16.4% of the variance conditionally and 0.3% marginally and fit better than the model containing only the participant random intercept, ΔR2 = .158, χ 2 (4) = 2659.02, p <.001. Variance was substantially larger for items (σ2 = .155) than for participants (σ2 = .007). Fixed effects are reported in Table 3. CR was not associated with the credibility ratings, CAM had a small negative association, and MFC had a very small positive association in the hypothesized direction. As this association was not found for accuracy and lies far below the smallest effect size of interest, the evidence for H2b is limited.

RQ2 Interactions CAM and Cognition

To test H4, we added the CAM x CR and CAM x MFC interactions to the accuracy and credibility models (Table 3). For accuracy, the CAM × CR interaction was significant (model R² = .10): Participants high in cognitive reflection were less accurate when they also held strong beliefs in alternative medicine (see Figure 1A).

RQ3 Intellectual Humility

Intellectual Humility was not significantly associated with accuracy, r = -.06, p = .290, 95% CI[-.16, .05]. The equivalence test Δr ± .17 indicated that this association was statistically equivalent to zero, 90% CI[-0.15, 0.03].

Controlling for CR, MFC, and CAM as covariates, intellectual humility had a significant but small association with the credibility ratings, β = 0.024, SE = 0.008, 95% CI [0.008, 0.041], t(338) = 2.87, p = .004 (Supplementary Table S1): More intellectually humble participants gave credibility ratings that were slightly more in line with the scientific evidence.

RQ4-RQ5 Conspiracy Belief and Trust in Science

Conspiracy belief was negatively associated with accuracy, r = -.24, 95% CI[-.34, -.14], p < .001, and in a multilevel model that also included trust in science, with credibility (β = -.035, SE = 0.010, 95% CI[-0.054, -0.016], t(340) = -3.58, p < .001): participants higher in conspiracy belief were thus less accurate when judging true and false information.

Trust in science was positively associated with accuracy, r = .14, 95% CI [.03, .24], p = .010 and with information-adjusted credibility in the same multilevel model, β = .020, SE = 0.010, 95% CI[0.001, 0.039], t(340) = 2.09, p = .038. Although the point estimate was slightly below our smallest effect size of interest, equivalence to zero could not be established, Δr ± .17, 90% CI[.05, .22], so the association cannot be dismissed as negligible.

In an exploratory robustness check including all individual-difference variables simultaneously, intellectual humility, CAM, and conspiracy belief remained significant predictors of credibility ratings, whereas trust in science did not, and the small association of MFC with credibility ratings (H2b) was no longer significant (β = .018, p = .256) (Supplementary Table S2).

RQ6 Predictors of Response Bias (c)

As shown in Table 1, c was significantly correlated with CAM, intellectual humility, trust in science, political orientation, and age, but not with conspiracy belief, CR, or MFC. Because lower values of c indicate a stronger tendency to judge information as true, participants with stronger belief in CAM, higher intellectual humility, higher trust in science, a more left-wing political orientation, and higher age therefore showed a more liberal response criterion. Entered simultaneously, these correlates explained 11.3% of the variance in c, F(5, 311) = 7.91, p < .001 (Supplementary Table 4). CAM, trust in science, and age remained significant predictors.

Intellectual humility and political orientation did not.

RQ7 Response Profiles

To describe response patterns beyond SDT indices, we classified each participant into one of nine response profiles based on their hit rate for true items and their false alarm rate for false items (see Methods). Figure 2 shows the distribution of participants across these profiles. Half of the participants (49.9%, n = 171) were classified as naive, accepting most true and most false information.

Discussion

Health misinformation spreads rapidly in online environments, yet it is still not well understood why some people believe incorrect health claims while others do not. We tested whether the ability and motivation to think effortfully and prior beliefs are related to how well people tell true from false health information (accuracy) and to how readily they accept claims in general (response bias). To this end, we presented a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population with correct and incorrect health claims based on real online information and analyzed participants' responses using a signal-detection approach. Contrary to our expectations, CR and MFC were unrelated to accuracy. Instead, stronger CAM and stronger conspiracy belief were related to lower accuracy. Trust in science showed a small positive association with accuracy and credibility that did not hold when controlling for the other belief variables, and intellectual humility was unrelated to accuracy. Participants with stronger CAM, higher trust in science and higher age accepted claims more readily. Taken together, this speaks against a simple lack-of-reflection account for health misinformation.

Surprisingly, neither the ability nor the motivation to reflect (captured by CR and MFC) was related to accuracy. This contradicts dual-process accounts, according to which people fall for misinformation because they fail to reflect [7, 17, 18], and contrasts with research on political news, where reflection is often associated with better discernment [16, 17, 40]. These findings may therefore not generalize to health information. One explanation might be that evaluating health information often requires medical and scientific knowledge that most laypeople lack.

Political news, on the other hand, is often part of everyday life and of direct concern for the people.

About half of the Austrian population has limited health literacy [57], finds it difficult to judge whether health information is trustworthy [58], and feels poorly informed about new medical discoveries [59]. Similarly, poor truth discernment has been linked not only to a lack of careful reasoning but also to a lack of relevant knowledge [18], and knowledge has been associated with better discrimination between true and fabricated news stories [60]. For health misinformation specifically, health literacy consistently predicted susceptibility, whereas cognitive reflection did so only for some health topics and self-reported reflection did not protect against it [31, 61]. Studies that did find effects of cognitive reflection on health misinformation mostly focused on COVID-19 (e.g., [11, 20, 41]). Because this topic received exceptionally extensive media coverage, it might resemble political news more than other health information. Health information also covers a much wider field and much of it may not be personally relevant (e.g., depending on age, gender, or medical conditions) and may thus give people little reason to think about it carefully, which could explain why motivation for cognition played no role.

Beliefs, in contrast, were by far the strongest predictors of accuracy. When judging political news, beliefs mainly shift response bias: people are more likely to judge a headline as true when it favors their own political identity, but they are not worse, if anything slightly better, at telling true from false headlines that favor their side [18]. In our study, by contrast, participants with stronger belief in CAM and conspiracy theories were worse at distinguishing correct from incorrect health claims. When people lack the knowledge to evaluate a health claim, they may fall back on what they already believe, even if these beliefs are inaccurate.

Notably, CAM predicted lower accuracy even though the incorrect claims did not particularly focus on alternative medicine. One possible explanation is that CAM is part of a broader set of beliefs: it is associated with a broader conspiratorial belief system [62]; in our data, too, conspiracy belief was associated with both CAM and lower accuracy. We also observed a small interaction: the negative association between CAM and accuracy was slightly stronger for more reflective participants. This can be explained with motivated reasoning [36], as analytical people tend to show a stronger bias toward belief-congruent information [40]. Given its small effect size, this interaction should be replicated, ideally with items designed to elicit a stronger belief-related bias.

When reasoning is unhelpful and people have to decide under uncertainty, their general tendency to accept or reject claims becomes important. Most of our participants showed a liberal response bias, that is, a tendency to judge information as "true" regardless of its veracity.

As half our claims were incorrect, this means that participants accepted many false claims along with the correct ones, and the largest group we identified was characterized by this "naive" tendency. This suggests a high general susceptibility to health misinformation in the Austrian population, driven mainly by a liberal response bias. Few studies have examined predictors of response bias in this context, and those that did found no reliable or only weak associations [20, 41]. In our study, stronger belief in alternative medicine, higher trust in science and higher age were robustly associated with a more liberal response bias.

Stronger CAM was associated not only with lower accuracy but also with a more liberal response bias. Belief in alternative medicine does not necessarily seem to be related to the rejection of scientific information (which we did not observe in our sample at all) but with a general tendency to accept all health claims, whether scientific or not.

Higher age was also associated with a more liberal response bias. In line with this, older adults also share considerably more fake news on social media than younger adults [63], possibly because they are less familiar with digital media and with how often false information circulates online [64].

Higher trust in science was likewise associated with a more liberal response bias.

Although increasing trust in science is a common goal in the face of science denial, our study shows that high trust in science can also have adverse effects. As we observed during material creation, false health claims often borrow scientific authority by referring to studies, using technical language or presenting complex pseudoscientific explanations. Trust in science without critical evaluation can therefore increase belief in incorrect claims [65]. Complex explanations can even make conspiracy theories more believable [35]. This means that interventions that merely tell people to look for "scientific credibility cues" (e.g., checking if there is a study quoted) are unlikely to improve discrimination if people lack the knowledge or literacy for critical evaluation.

Because evaluating claims through reasoning requires scientific and medical knowledge, one option would be to improve this knowledge directly. But given how broad the field of health information is, this hardly seems feasible. A more realistic approach would be behavioral interventions that change what people do when they encounter health claims. As people generally tend to accept rather than reject information, such interventions could raise awareness that much online health information may be false and, at the same time, teach people how to find and use verified fact-checking websites, such as medizin-transparent.at in Austria.

Raising awareness alone can increase general skepticism: exposure to fact-checks, tips for spotting fake news or news coverage of misinformation can reduce belief in incorrect claims but also in correct ones [8], and gamified inoculation interventions mainly led people to respond "false" to all news items [66]. This skepticism is not necessarily harmful, however.

Unlike participants in these studies, people who are unsure about a claim can seek out further information before accepting or rejecting it. Combined with the skills to check claims, a more skeptical stance could thus improve discrimination instead of leading people to dismiss accurate information. Finally, the response-profile grouping approach used in this study could help to tailor interventions to individuals: for example, people who recognize correct information but guess when judging incorrect information would benefit most from education targeting incorrect claims in particular.

In contrast to most previous research, which used political news or focused on COVID-19, our health-information items covered a wide range of health topics that were not tied to temporary events, which increases the generalizability of our findings. Some limitations should nonetheless be noted. First, participants judged each claim in a forced-choice format, without the option to look up further information. The liberal response bias in particular may therefore partly reflect guessing under uncertainty, which people can avoid outside the experimental setting provided they have the knowledge and motivation to seek out verified information.

Second, our design was correlational, so we have to be careful when interpreting causality.

People who find it difficult to evaluate health information may also be more drawn to alternative medicine or conspiracy theories, or both may depend on a third variable such as health literacy. Future studies could measure health literacy or medical knowledge to test whether reflection improves accuracy only when relevant knowledge is available. They could also give participants the option to seek out further information, which would show whether the liberal response bias reflects actual belief or guessing under uncertainty. Finally, intervention studies could test whether combining awareness of health misinformation with verification skills improves discrimination without increasing general skepticism.

Conclusion

How well people discern correct from incorrect health information is related more to what they believe than to how much they reflect, especially belief in alternative medicine was associated with lower accuracy. At the same time, most people tend to accept health claims regardless of their veracity, which implies a high general susceptibility to health misinformation. This tendency was stronger among people with stronger belief in alternative medicine, higher trust in science and higher age. Rather than encouraging reflection or trust in science, interventions should therefore build on these correlates and teach people how to accurately discriminate health information without undermining trust in accurate information.
